subject: mathematics_2a
question_text: If the point P denotes the complex number z = x + iy in the Argand plane and if (z − i)/(z − 1) is a purely imaginary number, find the locus of P.

mark_split.label: Write the quotient in terms of x and y
Multiply by the conjugate and separate real and imaginary parts
Set the real part to zero and state the locus

recall_prompt: Say how you would find the locus — what you substitute for z, what you multiply by, and which part you set to zero and why.
insider_note: Purely imaginary means the real part is 0 — setting the imaginary part to zero answers a different question. The last mark needs the locus as an equation in x and y, with the positive denominator dropped: x² + y² − x − y = 0.

steps.label: Substitute z = x + iy
steps.margin_note: First mark. Put z = x + iy in and group each of the top and bottom as (real) + i(imaginary). The −i on top joins the y; the −1 below joins the x.
steps.memory_tip: The −i on top joins the y; the −1 below joins the x. Group each as (real) + i(imaginary).

recall.must_convey: That z = x + iy is substituted so the quotient becomes [x + i(y − 1)] over [(x − 1) + iy].
accept: put z equals x plus i y so the top is x plus i times y minus one and the bottom is x minus one plus i y
substitute x plus i y for z and group real and imaginary parts above and below
the fraction becomes x plus i y minus one over x minus one plus i y
z ki x plus i y pettithe numerator x plus i y minus one, denominator x minus one plus i y
write numerator and denominator each as real plus i imaginary
reject: write it in x and y

steps.why: A locus is an equation in x and y, so z has to become x + iy before anything can be said. Grouping the real and imaginary parts now is what makes the conjugate in the next step easy to write.
common_mistakes: Grouping the −i with x instead of with iy.
Writing the denominator as x − 1 + y, dropping the i.

steps.label: Multiply by the conjugate
steps.margin_note: Half the marks. The conjugate of the denominator is (x − 1) − iy. The denominator becomes (x − 1)² + y², a real number; the numerator's real part is x(x − 1) + y(y − 1) and it is the only thing needed next.
steps.memory_tip: The conjugate of (x − 1) + iy is (x − 1) − iy. Only the numerator's real part is needed.
lines: Multiply above and below by (x − 1) − iy:
∴ real part = (x² + y² − x − y)/((x − 1)² + y²)

recall.must_convey: That multiplying by the conjugate (x − 1) − iy makes the denominator real and gives real part (x² + y² − x − y) over (x − 1)² + y².
accept: multiply by the conjugate x minus one minus i y, the denominator becomes x minus one squared plus y squared and the real part on top is x squared plus y squared minus x minus y
rationalise the denominator and separate the real part x squared plus y squared minus x minus y
after multiplying by the conjugate the real part of the numerator is x squared plus y squared minus x minus y
conjugate tho multiply chesi real part x square plus y square minus x minus y teeyali
make the denominator real with the conjugate and collect the real terms
heard_as: x minus one minus i y

steps.why: 'Purely imaginary' is a statement about the real part, and the real part of a quotient can only be read once the denominator is real. The conjugate does exactly that, and the expansion is the price.
common_mistakes: Using (x − 1) + iy as the 'conjugate' — the sign of the i term must flip.
Spending time simplifying the imaginary part, which is not used.

steps.label: Real part = 0
steps.margin_note: Last mark. Purely imaginary means the real part is 0. The denominator is positive, so only the numerator has to vanish.
steps.memory_tip: Purely imaginary means the REAL part is 0. The denominator is positive, so only the numerator must vanish.

lines.text: ∴ Locus of P: x² + y² − x − y = 0

recall.must_convey: That a purely imaginary number has real part zero, so x² + y² − x − y = 0 is the locus of P.
accept: purely imaginary means real part zero so the locus is x squared plus y squared minus x minus y equals zero
set the real part to zero and the locus is x squared plus y squared minus x minus y equals zero
the numerator of the real part must be zero, that is the locus
purely imaginary ante real part zero, so x square plus y square minus x minus y equals zero
real part equals zero gives the circle x squared plus y squared minus x minus y equals zero
heard_as: x squared plus y squared minus x minus y

steps.why: The condition in the question is used exactly once, here. A purely imaginary number is 0 + i(something), so its real part is 0 — and the resulting equation is a circle through the origin. The point z = 1 itself is not on the locus because the quotient is undefined there; the board answer is the circle's equation.
common_mistakes: Setting the imaginary part to zero — that is the condition for 'purely real'.
Leaving the denominator in the final answer.
Writing the answer as an inequality or as x² + y² = x + y with no '= 0' form — either is fine, but the standard form is expected.
